tx.t: Let me tell you something about the history and the economics of coffee. According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder called Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became lively after eating the berries.

By the fifteenth century, coffee was grown in Yemen, and it then spread to Turkey and Europe. There are two main kinds of coffee, Arabica and Robusta, and about sixty per cent of the world's coffee is Arabica.
Brazil produces about one third of the world's coffee, more than any other country. People around the world drink about two billion cups of coffee every day.

tx.t: In today's lecture, I will talk about the growth of cities. In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's people lived in cities.
The United Nations expects the figure to reach about two thirds by twenty fifty. Cities take up only about two per cent of the Earth's land, but they produce most of the world's wealth.
Rapid growth can cause housing shortages, traffic jams and air pollution. Some cities are planting trees and building cycle lanes to make urban life healthier.

tx.t: Today I want to explain why sleep is so important, and what happens in the brain during the night. Adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, while teenagers need eight to ten.

A full cycle of sleep lasts about ninety minutes, and we go through four or five cycles each night. Most vivid dreams happen during a stage called REM sleep, when the eyes move quickly under the eyelids.

While we sleep, the brain moves memories from short-term storage into long-term storage. Lack of sleep makes it harder to concentrate and slows reaction times, which is why tired drivers cause many accidents.
On average, people spend about one third of their lives asleep.

By twenty ten, the number had risen to three hundred and ninety-six pairs, which shows that careful management can work.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe the world's rainforests and why scientists want to protect them. Rainforests cover only about six per cent of the Earth's land surface.
However, they are home to more than half of all the plant and animal species on land. The Amazon is the largest rainforest, and it spreads across nine countries.
A rainforest has four main layers: the emergent layer, the canopy, the understorey and the forest floor. Most animals live in the canopy, where there is plenty of light and fruit.
Many modern medicines come from rainforest plants, and scientists believe thousands more are still unknown.

tx.t: This week we are studying the life of Marie Curie, one of the most important scientists of the twentieth century. She was born in Warsaw in eighteen sixty-seven and moved to Paris to study when she was twenty-four.

Together with her husband Pierre, she discovered two new elements, polonium and radium, in eighteen ninety-eight. In nineteen oh three she won the Nobel Prize in Physics, becoming the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize.
In nineteen eleven she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry. During the First World War, she developed mobile X-ray units that doctors used to treat wounded soldiers.
She died in nineteen thirty-four, probably because of her long exposure to radiation.

tx.t: Researchers at Redbridge University carried out a study in twenty seventeen to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed three hundred and sixty-seven students over eleven weeks.
On average, the students studied for three hours a day. However, only fifty-nine per cent of them used any planned method.
The students who used the method of studying at the same time each day felt less stressed before the exam. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.
